name: Occam’s Razor
description: When two explanations or designs solve the same problem equally well, prefer the simpler one with fewer assumptions. In UX discourse, it is often invoked as shorthand for removing needless complexity.
design_relevance_note: Shows up in feature-trimming, interaction simplification, and information-architecture debates where designers argue against adding extra states, controls, or explanatory machinery.
myth_risk_note: Occam's Razor is widely invoked as a general principle for theory choice, but the only on-topic evidence found is narrowly mathematical (Bayesian model selection), not evidence about whether preferring simplicity is epistemically justified in general -- consistent with this entry's existing no_rigorous_backing_found status.
prevalence_note: Dedicated Laws of UX entry and frequently cited in design-simplification/product-thinking articles, but usually as borrowed reasoning guidance rather than a first-order HCI law.

applications.title: Criminal-defense attorney Scott Greenfield's KISS courtroom strategy
applications.description: Criminal-defense attorney Scott Greenfield advocates a 'Keep It Simple, Stupid' courtroom strategy modeled directly on Occam's razor: when a client's guilt on the facts is not seriously in dispute, Greenfield argues the winning approach is to accept the straightforward facts rather than contest or over-explain them, since piling on contested points and explanations tends to make a defense look more complicated -- and less credible -- than the simpler account.
applications.industry_context: legal / criminal defense (not a digital-product context)
applications.ethical_note: A professional decision-making heuristic with no persuasion-of-end-users dimension -- it concerns how an attorney frames a legal argument, not how a product or interface influences a user. Included despite being outside this corpus's usual product/UX context because Occam's Razor itself is a general-reasoning heuristic, not a UX pattern, and this is the strongest real, named, attributable illustration found of someone actually applying it as an explicit operating principle rather than merely being cited as a truism.
